title: Why Grease Blockages Form in Kitchen Sinks
description: When liquid fats, oils, and grease (FOG) are poured down a kitchen sink, they flow easily while warm. However, as FOG moves into the drainage system, it cools rapidly upon contact with cold wastewater and pipe walls. Over time, solidified grease coats the interior of the P-trap and horizontal drain lines, trapping food particles and gradually restricting flow until a full blockage occurs. To prevent chronic drain issues, wipe greasy pans with paper towels before washing and dispose of cooled oils in solid waste bins. What is your go-to method for clearing grease-choked sink lines?

visual_story: The visual uses a clear pipe cutaway to demonstrate what happens inside a drain when fats, oils, and grease enter the system. Viewers can see the congealed grease clinging to the bottom and side walls of the P-trap, demonstrating how liquid waste turns into a physical restriction as it cools. This visual reinforces why grease shouldn't go down the drain even if it appears completely liquid in the sink.

on_image_text.hook: Why Liquid Grease Still Blocks Sinks
on_image_text.explanation: Warm fats cool inside pipes, solidifying into solid wall deposits that trap waste.
on_image_text.takeaway: Scrape greasy cookware into solid trash before washing to prevent blockages.
